what: The one failure of the ABR suite in the stability runs: PB-ABR-006 in Firefox in the Playwright image, one run of three. Condensed from the attachments of the failed attempt (qa-events.json, qa-metrics.json, request-log.json); nothing was edited.

environment.host: Apple M2 Pro, 12 cores, shared with other agents (load average 15 to 21 during the run)
environment.command: PB_PORT=4670 npm run docker:pw -- --cpus 3 npx playwright test tests/e2e/abr.spec.ts --project=firefox --workers=2 --repeat-each=3

failure: rebuffers in the first 10 s of playback (metrics.rebuffer.events): at most one, saw 2: at media time 8.01 s for 24 ms; at media time 9.97 s for 358 ms
readThisWay: The link is 600 kbps and carries only the 240p rung. The player started on 360p (index 4), was cut off after 133 kB and stepped down to 240p 2.0 s after the load was requested (index 6), as in every other run: the first frame came at 3.1 s. The `t` of the events is the page clock, ms, and the first event, load-requested, is at 354.

4.2 s after the load was requested (index 10, media time 0.52 s), 2.2 s after the step down and well inside Shaka's 8 s switch interval, the player moved UP to 360p, reason abr. The request log agrees (the 240p segment 3 was cut off at once, 360p segment 3 asked for): the rung is a real one, not an artefact of the hook.
360p needs 764 kbps and the link gives 600: each 360p segment took 2.3 to 2.5 s for 2 s of video, and the player rebuffered at media times 8.01 s, 9.97 s and 11.99 s.

13 of 366 decoded frames were dropped in the load (3.6 %); the hook does not say when. Shaka disables the variant that is playing for 30 s when 15 % of the frames of a 2 s window are dropped (abr.droppedFrames, on by default); Player.disableStream then chooses a variant again at once (chooseVariantAndSwitch_, a `variantchanged` that the hook records as abr), and nothing in that path is held back by the switch interval. A ban of 240p leaves only 360p and 720p, and the player takes the lower. This is the one explanation found that fits the evidence; it was NOT reproduced (Chromium under a 4x and 8x CPU throttle did not drop frames at 240p), and ten more Firefox runs of the same test passed with 0 dropped frames each.
